clinicalPearls: Functional cysts arise from normal ovulatory physiology; the two principal types are follicular cysts, from failure of a dominant follicle to rupture, and corpus luteum cysts, from failure of the corpus luteum to regress.
They are the commonest ovarian cysts in reproductive-age women and the great majority resolve spontaneously over two to three menstrual cycles.
Most are asymptomatic but may cause unilateral pelvic pain, menstrual disturbance, or acute pain if rupture or intracystic haemorrhage occurs.
A simple, unilocular, anechoic, thin-walled cyst below the usual size threshold in a premenopausal woman is almost always benign and managed expectantly.
A corpus luteum cyst may bleed, causing acute pain and occasionally haemoperitoneum, a risk that is heightened in women taking anticoagulants.
Ovarian torsion is the key emergency and its likelihood rises with larger cysts.
Theca lutein cysts are functional cysts driven by high beta-hCG, seen in molar pregnancy, multiple gestation and ovulation induction.
Combined hormonal contraception does not hasten resolution of an existing cyst but reduces the formation of new functional cysts.
reference.pathophysiology: During each cycle a dominant follicle matures under follicle-stimulating and luteinising hormone drive; when such a follicle fails to rupture and continues to accumulate fluid, a follicular cyst forms. After ovulation the corpus luteum normally involutes, and if it instead persists or fills with fluid or blood, a corpus luteum cyst results. These lesions are physiological and hormonally responsive rather than neoplastic, and most involute once the hormonal stimulus wanes. Theca lutein cysts represent bilateral functional enlargement from excessive human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation.
additionalDifferentials: Benign ovarian neoplasm such as serous cystadenoma or mature cystic teratoma
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to assess morphology, size and Doppler flow
Serum beta-hCG to exclude pregnancy or ectopic and to explain theca lutein cysts
Full blood count where haemorrhage is suspected
CA-125 interpreted with caution in premenopausal women, ideally within a risk-of-malignancy index or IOTA rules
Interval ultrasound to confirm spontaneous resolution
Germ-cell and sex-cord tumour markers in young women with complex lesions
redFlags: Acute severe unilateral pain with features of torsion, constituting a surgical emergency
Haemodynamic instability or signs of haemoperitoneum from a ruptured haemorrhagic cyst
Complex, solid or multilocular morphology or persistence, raising suspicion of neoplasm
Any ovarian cyst in a postmenopausal woman, in whom functional cysts should not occur
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with the large majority of functional cysts resolving spontaneously and requiring no intervention. Complications such as torsion or haemorrhage are uncommon and readily treatable.
pitfalls: Labelling a persistent or complex cyst as functional without confirmatory follow-up imaging.
Assuming a cyst in a postmenopausal woman is functional rather than investigating it.
Over-reliance on CA-125 in premenopausal women, in whom it is raised by endometriosis, fibroids and pelvic infection.
Missing an ectopic pregnancy by not checking beta-hCG in a woman with pain and an adnexal mass.
Delaying surgery in suspected torsion while awaiting further imaging.
references: RCOG/BSGE Green-top Guideline: Management of suspected ovarian masses in premenopausal women
IOTA (International Ovarian Tumour Analysis) simple rules
management: Expectant management with reassurance, as most functional cysts resolve spontaneously over a few menstrual cycles
Simple analgesia for associated pelvic pain
Interval transvaginal ultrasound to confirm resolution of a simple cyst
Combined hormonal contraception to reduce the formation of new functional cysts in recurrent cases
Exclude pregnancy and ectopic with beta-hCG and apply malignancy risk assessment for complex lesions
Recognise and urgently manage ovarian torsion and significant intracystic haemorrhage or haemoperitoneum, with detorsion or ovarian-sparing cystectomy
Refer for gynaecological or surgical assessment when a cyst is persistent, enlarging, complex or symptomatic
